data.caption: soovera.com
data.copy:
I was diagnosed with Ménière's disease at 51. I'm 58 now. Turns out I never had Ménière's at all.

For seven years, I "managed" a condition without understanding what was actually driving it.

But every year, I felt myself shrinking a little more.

Seven years of diuretics that made me exhausted and dehydrated.

Seven years of low-sodium diets that made every meal bland and joyless.

Seven years of vestibular therapy that never actually helped.

Seven years of being told "it's Ménière's, this is chronic, you'll manage it for life."

I did everything they asked.

When that didn't work, they sent me for more tests.

VNG test with those black goggles. Positive for Ménière's.

Audiogram. Slight hearing loss in my left ear. MRI. Normal. They said that confirmed it.

"Classic Ménière's," they said. "Your inner ear fluid is out of balance."

I felt broken. Like my body had turned against me.

Some days the ringing was so loud I couldn't hear my husband talking across the kitchen table.

That constant fullness in my ears. Like they were packed with cotton I couldn't pull out.

The dizziness wasn't severe spinning. Just a persistent, floating sensation that made me feel unsteady on my feet.

And every single morning, I'd wake up with my sinuses completely congested.

Pressure across my cheeks and forehead. Heavy. Thick. Never fully lifting.

But nobody connected those two things.

The sinus congestion was "just allergies."

The ear pressure and ringing? "That's your Ménière's."

Two separate problems, they said.

I stopped going to movies because the noise made the ringing unbearable.

I'd sit in restaurants and nod along to conversations I couldn't actually hear over the high-pitched screaming in my ears.

I stopped going to my book club because the room would tilt slightly whenever I stood up, and I couldn't follow the discussion over the ringing.

I planned every day around how congested I'd wake up and how loud the ringing would be.

And every doctor just nod…

data.caption: casaandbeyond.com
data.copy:
At some point in your fifties you stop tolerating things that aren't right.

Not in an unreasonable way.

Just — life is short, my home is my sanctuary, and I've earned the right to have exactly what I want in it.

I stopped buying things because they were fine.
I stopped keeping things because replacing them felt wasteful.
I stopped settling for "close enough" in a space I spend most of my time in.

The blanket situation had been bothering me for two years.

I had one that was technically acceptable — inoffensive print, reasonable quality — but it wasn't the right piece and I knew it every time I walked into the bedroom.

There's a specific low-grade dissatisfaction that comes from a room that's almost right.

Like a word on the tip of your tongue.

Maddening.

I'm particular about textiles.

I follow several interior creators whose aesthetic aligns with mine — English cottage, grandmillennial, warm botanicals, rooms that look like they've been collected over decades rather than ordered from a catalogue in an afternoon.

When one of them showed the Casa & Beyond cotton blanket in her bedroom, I knew immediately.

It's the kind of print you'd pay three times the price for at a specialty linen store.

Rich botanical design.
Warm earthy tones.
Reversible — so you get two looks depending on what the room needs that season.

And it's 100% cotton — genuinely — which means it washes properly, breathes properly, and improves with age rather than deteriorating.

It arrived exactly as shown.

That matters more than people realise when you've been burned by the gap between photography and reality.

The colours were the colours.
The weight was substantial.

It went on the bed and the room was settled.

I've already sent the link to three friends.

Two have ordered.

That's the only review that counts.

data.copy:
If you're already on blood pressure medication, already on a statin, and your er*ctions are still getting weaker, your energy is still dropping, and your doctor just keeps adjusting doses and sending you home. I need to tell you something that took me 23 years of reading cardiac imaging to fully understand.

I'm Dr. Mike Harris, a cardiologist specialising in preventive cardiology and endothelial dysfunction.

And I need to tell you about the canary.

Coal miners used to carry canaries into the mine. Not as pets. As a warning system. When the canary died, there was toxic gas in the tunnel. The miners couldn't see it, couldn't smell it. But the canary felt it first, because it was the most sensitive creature in the room.

Your er*ctions are the canary.

Your penile arteries are 1 to 2 millimetres wide. Your coronary arteries are 3 to 4 millimetres. When plaque starts building system-wide, it shows up in the smallest vessels first. Years before your heart feels a thing.

Researchers have called ED "the earliest clinical manifestation of systemic vascular disease" [Princeton Consensus Panel, 2003]. ED doesn't appear after heart disease. It appears before it. The canary dies in the bedroom before the gas ever reaches the heart.

Most men I see are already doing everything right on paper. Blood pressure controlled. Cholesterol managed. Numbers within range. They're compliant patients.

And they're still getting worse.

Still exhausted. Still watching their er*ctions quietly fade a little more each year.

Because managing a number on a chart is not the same as fixing the circulation that feeds every organ in your body.

Controlling a reading is not the same as healing a vessel. And nobody in mainstream medicine has time to explain the difference.

I know this because at 49, I was that man.

My numbers were managed. But I was exhausted in a way that sleep didn't fix. Morning er*ctions, gone for almost a year.

And when my wife looked at me, I saw the shift I'd been dreadin…

I did facials on twin sisters yesterday for their 60th birthday and under my exam lamp, one looked 10 years younger than the other. When I asked what she was doing differently, she showed me the one thing I'd been telling clients to avoid for years.

I felt like a massive idiot.

I've been doing facials for 22 years.

I've seen every skin type, every concern, every level of damage.

I can tell within 30 seconds of looking at someone's face what treatments they need.

Yesterday, I couldn't.

Twin sisters came in. Booked appointments for their 60th birthday. Wanted to treat themselves.

They sat in my waiting room together, laughing, finishing each other's sentences.

I took Jennifer back first.

Put her under my exam lamp to assess her skin.

And I just stopped.

Her skin looked deflated. Dehydrated. That dull, flat quality I see on most women her age.

Texture was rough. Pores looked enlarged because the skin around them had lost structure.

That exhausted look. Like someone turned down the brightness on her face.

Nothing unusual. This is what I see every single day.

Then I brought her sister Karen back.

Same genes. Same family. Same age to the day.

I put her under the same lamp.

Her skin looked completely different.

Plump. Dewy. That hydrated-from-within quality I usually only see after treatments, not before.

Her pores were refined. Her texture was smooth. Her skin had this brightness that doesn't just happen naturally at 60.

At 60, both sisters are post-menopausal. That's when estrogen drops and collagen loss accelerates by up to 30% in just the first five years.

That's not gradual aging. That's a hormonal cliff.

But only one of them looked like she'd fallen off it.

I looked at Jennifer's intake form. Then at Karen's. Same birthday. Twins.

But their skin looked a decade apart.

They usually age similarly. Maybe one takes slightly better care of herself. Uses sunscreen more. Smokes less.

data.copy:
My son-in-law rolled his eyes when my grandson asked me to explain Revelation, but he stopped smiling when I began to answer…

It was Sunday lunch. The kind of meal where three generations gather around the same table and pretend everything is fine.

My daughter was clearing plates. Her husband, Brian, was scrolling through his phone. And my grandson, Luke, nine years old, was flipping through the children's Bible I'd given him for his birthday.

"Grandma," he said, "what's the book of Revelation about?"

I froze. Fork halfway to my mouth.

Brian looked up from his phone and smirked. Not even a hidden smirk. A full, obvious, "here we go" smirk.

"Grandma's been going to church for forty years, buddy," he said. "I'm sure she can explain Revelation."

The way he said it. Like he was daring me. Like he already knew I couldn't.

My daughter shot him a look, but she didn't say a word.

She just stood there with a stack of plates in her hands, waiting to see if I'd answer or dodge the question like I always did.

I'd been a Christian my entire adult life. 41 years.

I'd taught Sunday school. I'd led women's Bible studies. I'd read through the entire Bible, cover to cover, at least a dozen times.

But if you'd asked me to explain Revelation, I would've smiled, said something vague about the end times and Jesus coming back, and steered the conversation somewhere else as fast as possible.

Luke was still looking at me. Waiting.

Brian leaned back in his chair, arms folded. He wasn't even pretending to be polite anymore. He wanted to watch me squirm.

I took a breath.

"Revelation," I said, "was written by the apostle John around AD 95. He'd been exiled to an island called Patmos by the Roman emperor because he wouldn't stop preaching about Jesus. While he was there, Jesus gave him a vision. And the very first thing Jesus told him to do was write letters to seven specific churches in Asia Minor."

Brian's smirk faded. Just slightly.

data.caption: soothecurawell.com
data.copy:
3:17 AM.
I know because I'm staring at the clock. Again.
My heart is hammering so hard I can feel it in my throat. The sheets are soaked through. My head is pounding with that familiar, sickening throb that starts behind my eyes and radiates down my neck.
And that taste. God, that taste in my mouth. Like something died in there.
========
But the worst part? The absolute worst part isn't physical.
It's the thoughts.
The spiraling, suffocating thoughts that come flooding in at 3AM when there's nothing to distract you from what you've become.
*Did I say something embarrassing at dinner?*
*Why did my husband give me that look?*
*Did I forget to pick up my daughter from soccer practice? No, wait... that was yesterday.*
*Or was it today?*
========
I reach for my phone. Thirteen unread messages. My stomach drops.
I'm too scared to open them. What if I sent something? What if I called someone? What if I don't remember?
========
This is my life now.
This is what I've become.
And the worst part? Tomorrow, I'll do it all over again.
========
**THE MORNING AFTER (EVERY MORNING AFTER)**
The alarm goes off at 6:30 AM.
I've had maybe two hours of actual sleep. The rest was just... sweaty, anxious half-consciousness punctuated by nightmares I can't quite remember.
I sit up slowly. The room spins.
My hands are shaking so badly I can barely turn off the alarm. I try three times before I manage to swipe correctly.
========
The bathroom mirror is not my friend anymore.
The face staring back at me is puffy. Bloated. My eyes are bloodshot, with dark circles so deep they look like bruises. My skin has this gray, lifeless quality that no amount of makeup can hide.
I'm 38 years old.
I look 52.
========
I grip the sink with both hands and try to breathe. Just breathe.
But my chest is tight. That familiar band of anxiety is already constricting around my ribs, making every breath feel incomplete.
*I can't do this again.*
*I can't keep living like this.*
But I will. Because I always do.
======…

activeadsgrowthperiod.description: Lookback window for active-ads growth filter.
activeadsgrowthperiod.allowed_values: 1w, 1m, 3m. Default 1m when min/max growth set. 1w=1 week, 1m=1 month, 3m=3 months.
activeadsgrowthperiod.notes: 14d/2m exist on the dashboard but are omitted from MCP — sparse wlads baselines return empty result sets.

minpagelikes.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. Ads missing the field excluded when min set.

minadspend.description: Minimum EU ad spend total in adspendtimeframe window.
minadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier; can return upgrade JSON.

maxadspend.description: Maximum EU ad spend in window.
maxadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. 999999 treated as no upper cap server-side.

adspendtimeframe.description: Rolling window ad spend is summed over (NOT a calendar month filter).

minreach.description: Minimum EU reach/views total in reachtimeframe window.
minreach.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

reachtimeframe.description: Rolling window reach is summed over.

mintraffic.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

minproductsonstore.description: Minimum published products on the Shopify store.

minprice.description: Minimum product price on landing page.

mincopylength.description: Minimum ad primary text character length.

minvideolength.description: Minimum video duration in seconds (use with mediafilter=videos).

mindays.description: Minimum days the ad has been running.
mindays.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

from.description: Ad launch date lower bound (Meta started field — when ad began running, NOT scrape date).
from.allowed_values: YYYY-MM-DD. Requires to on same range.

to.notes: To isolate ads running in a calendar month: ad_created_to=last day of month AND fromlastseen=first day of month.

product_from.description: Shopify product creation date lower bound.

pagefrom.description: Facebook page creation date lower bound.

activestatus.description: Legacy dashboard param (no longer applied to ES queries).
activestatus.allowed_values: Ignored — use adstatus or last_seen_from/to instead.

adstatus.description: Dashboard Status filter — recently seen vs stale ads.
adstatus.allowed_values: active (lastSeen or updated_at within last 4 days), inactive (neither field within last 4 days), All/empty (no status filter).
adstatus.notes: find_winning_products forces active. Same as dashboard Status = Active.

sorting.allowed_values: relevance, datefound, mostrecent, lastseen, adspend, longestrunning, reach, adsetamount, consistency, monthlyvisits, monthlytraffic, monthlyrevenue, pageactiveads, toprank, mostsaved. Aliases: rank/top_ad/best_ranked→toprank (asc = best rank first, desc = worst rank first). ad_started→mostrecent. monthly_visits→monthlyvisits. monthly_traffic→monthlytraffic.

page.description: Pagination page index (informational). Deep pagination requires scroll from the previous response — incrementing page alone does not advance the result set.
page.allowed_values: MCP uses 1-based page (1=first page); echoed value is 0-based internal page sent to API.

scroll.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Empty/omit on the first request; pass the response scroll value on the next request with the same filters to fetch more ads. Required to download beyond the first page (especially sort_by=lastseen).
scroll.allowed_values: Opaque string from previous response; empty string or omit for first page. Stop when scroll is null/absent or data is shorter than a full page.

KB Back In Stock Restock Alert
Sticky Add To Cart Booster Pro
POWR Email Popup Sales Pop Ups
EG Auto Add to Cart Free Gift
SA Request a Quote, Hide Price

mcp_pagination.hint: Pass scroll_next as scroll on the next call with the same filters to continue. Do not rely on page alone.
